{{Short description|Mathematical constant related to the cosine function}}
[[file:Cosine_fixed_point.svg|thumb|The Dottie number is the unique real [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] of the [[cosine]] function.]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''Dottie number''' or the '''cosine constant''' is a [[mathematical constant|constant]] that is the unique [[real number|real]] root of the equation
<math display="block"> \cos x = x ,</math>
where the argument of <math>\cos</math> is in [[radian]]s.

The decimal expansion of the Dottie number is given by:
{{indent|5}}
{{math|1=''D'' = {{val|0.739085133215160641655312087673}}...}} {{OEIS|id=A003957}}.

Since <math>\cos(x) - x</math> is [[monotonic function|decreasing]] and its [[derivative]] is non-zero at <math>\cos(x) - x = 0</math>, it only crosses zero at one point. This implies that the equation <math>\cos(x) = x</math> has only one real solution. It is the single [[real-valued]] [[fixed point (mathematics)|fixed point]] of the [[cosine]] function and is a [[triviality (mathematics)|nontrivial]] example of a universal attracting fixed point. It is also a [[transcendental number]] because of the [[Lindemann–Weierstrass theorem]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://mathworld.wolfram.com/DottieNumber.html|author=Eric W. Weisstein|authorlink=Eric W. Weisstein|title=Dottie Number}}</ref> The generalised case <math> \cos z = z </math> for a complex variable <math> z </math> has infinitely many roots, but unlike the Dottie number, they are not attracting fixed points.

[[file:quadrisection.svg|thumb|The solution of quadrisection of circle into four parts of the same area with chords coming from the same point can be expressed via Dottie number.]]

== History ==
The constant appeared in publications as early as 1860s.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |title=Dottie Number |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/DottieNumber.html |access-date=2025-01-29 |website=mathworld.wolfram.com |language=en}}</ref> [[Norair Arakelian]] used lowercase [[Ayb (Armenian letter)|ayb]] (ա) from the [[Armenian alphabet]] to denote the constant.<ref name=":0" />

The constant name was coined by Samuel R. Kaplan in 2007. It originates from a professor of French named Dottie who observed the number by repeatedly pressing the cosine button on her calculator.<ref name="Kaplan" />{{refn|group=nb|If a calculator is set to take angles in [[degree (angle)|degrees]], the sequence of numbers will instead converge to <math>0.999847...</math>,<ref>{{Cite OEIS|A330119}}</ref> the root of <math>\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{180}x\right) = x</math>.}}

The Dottie number, for which an exact series expansion can be obtained using the [[Faà di Bruno formula]], has interesting connections with the Kepler and Bertrand's circle problems.<ref name="pain2023">{{cite arXiv |last=Pain |first=Jean-Christophe |date=2023 |title=An exact series expansion for the Dottie number |class=math.NT |eprint=2303.17962}}</ref>

==Identities==
The Dottie number appears in the closed form expression of some [[integral]]s:<ref>{{Citation |last=Michos |first=Alexander |title=A Brief Investigation of an Integral Representation of Dottie's Number |date=2023-03-03 |url=https://osf.io/3rzj5 |access-date=2024-09-24 |doi=10.31219/osf.io/3rzj5}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Integral Representation of the Dottie Number |url=https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/2446725/integral-representation-of-the-dottie-number |website=Mathematics Stack Exchange |language=en}}</ref>
<math display="block">\int _0^\infty\ln \left(\frac{4\left(x+\sinh x\right)^2+\pi^2}{4(x-\sinh x)^2+\pi ^2}\right){\rm d}x = \pi^2 - 2\pi D</math>
<math display="block">\int_{0 }^\infty \frac{3\pi^2+4(x-\sinh x)^2}{(3\pi^2+4(x-\sinh x)^2)^2 + 16\pi^2(x-\sinh x)^2}\,{\rm d}x = \frac1{8+8\sqrt{1-D^2}} </math>

Using the [[Taylor series]] of the inverse of <math>f(x) = \cos(x) - x</math> at <math display="inline">\frac{\pi}{2}</math> (or equivalently, the [[Lagrange inversion theorem]]), the Dottie number can be expressed as the [[infinite series]]:
<math display="block"> D = \frac{\pi}{2}+\sum_{n\,\mathrm{odd}} a_n \pi^{n}</math> 
where each <math>a_n</math> is a [[rational number]] defined for odd {{mvar|n}} as<ref name="Kaplan">{{cite journal |last1=Kaplan |first1=Samuel R |date=February 2007 |title=The Dottie Number |url=https://www.maa.org/sites/default/files/Kaplan2007-131105.pdf |journal=Mathematics Magazine |volume=80 |page=73 |doi=10.1080/0025570X.2007.11953455 |s2cid=125871044 |accessdate=29 November 2017}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=OEIS A302977 Numerators of the rational factor of Kaplan's series for the Dottie number. |url=https://oeis.org/A302977 |access-date=2019-05-26 |website=oeis.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=A306254 - OEIS |url=https://oeis.org/A306254 |access-date=2019-07-22 |website=oeis.org}}</ref>{{refn|group=nb|Kaplan does not give an explicit formula for the terms of the series, which follows trivially from the [[Lagrange inversion theorem]].}}
<math display="block">\begin{align}
a_n&=\frac{1}{n!2^n}\lim_{m\to\frac\pi2}
\frac{\partial^{n-1}}{\partial m^{n-1}}{\left(\frac{\cos m}{m-\pi/2}-1\right)^{-n}}
\\&=-\frac{1}{4},-\frac{1}{768},-\frac{1}{61440},-\frac{43}{165150720},\ldots
\end{align}</math>

The Dottie number can also be expressed as:
<math display="block">D=\sqrt{1-\left(1-2I^{-1}_\frac12\left(\frac 12,\frac 32\right)\right)^2},</math>
where <math>I^{-1}</math> is the inverse of the regularized [[beta function]]. This value can be obtained using [[Kepler's equation]], along with other equivalent closed forms. <math>I^{-1}_\frac12\left(\tfrac 12,\tfrac 32\right) \approx 0.16319</math> is the median of a [[beta distribution]] with parameters 1/2 and 3/2. 
<ref name="pain2023" />

In [[Microsoft Excel]], Open Office and LibreOffice Calc spreadsheets, the Dottie number can be expressed in closed form as {{code|SQRT(1-(1-2*BETA.INV(1/2,1/2,3/2))^2)|dax|style=white-space:nowrap}}. In the [[Mathematica]] [[computer algebra]] system, the Dottie number is {{code|Sqrt[1 - (1-2 InverseBetaRegularized[1/2, 1/2, 3/2])^2]|mathematica|style=white-space:nowrap}}.

Another closed form representation: 
<math display="block">D=- \tanh\left(2\operatorname{arctanh}\left(\frac1{\sqrt3} \operatorname{InvT} \left(\frac14,3\right)\right)\right)=-\frac{2\sqrt3 {\operatorname{InvT}\left(\frac14,3\right)}}{\operatorname{InvT}^2\left(\frac14,3\right)+3},</math>
where <math>\operatorname{InvT}</math> is the inverse survival function of [[Student's t-distribution]]. In Microsoft Excel, Open Office and LibreOffice Calc, due to the specifics of the realization of <code>TINV</code> function, this can be expressed as formulas {{code|2 *SQRT(3)* TINV(1/2, 3)/(TINV(1/2, 3)^2+3)|dax|style=white-space:nowrap}} and {{code|TANH(2*ATANH(1/SQRT(3) * TINV(1/2,3)))|dax|style=white-space:nowrap}}.
